content: So, in that respect, the ML lectures are absolutely worth it. They're a tool to empower you, not a cheat code.
Markets are adversarial. It's like Kung Fu. You're not the only one training, your opponents also are.

This is an ___active research field___ whose very mathematical nature obliges us to be creative in ways that no textbook can tell you. The point of learning theory is to empower us with the tools and intuitions necessary to survive more easily.

There is no single source of knowledge that will tell you exactly what the cheat code is, because the very nature of leaking the cheat code causes it to disappear. This is as true for ML as it is for technical analysis or fundamentals or economics.

The biggest misconception that I fear people might have is that Finance is about learning enough theory and then retiring. By the very definition of market efficiency and alpha decay, ***this is not possible***

referenced_message.content: So the course on ML on skool isnt worth it?

content: The point of the ML course is to direct you into the domains where it actually works.
The course on ML is "not worth it" only if your preconception is an immature expectation that you can immediately import xgboost and have it predict tomorrow's price.
So the course on ML on skool isnt worth it?

My personal opinion is to actually learn the theory and to start simple: moving averages, volatility sizing, ranked asset allocation, and so on. No amount of LLM-induced ML slop will substitute actual domain knowledge intuition.

This ability to "divine" new knowledge remains an unsolved mystery of the human mind. Statistically speaking, the probability of discovering strategies that work is effectively 0, on account of the sheer size of the parameter space. And yet, human beings can accomplish what millions of genetic algorithm iterations cannot: a true measure of perception.

As it stands, LLMs too remain patently unable to magically give you the financial models you need. Why? Because LLMs can take a corpus of knowledge 1000s of times larger than you'll ever read and interpolate between them, but they are incapable of genuine novel breakthroughs. If they appear to do so, it is only because they're putting pre-existing puzzle pieces together, ***not*** because they've divined a genuine new source of knowledge.
And it is ***that*** which is the actual secret sauce: the ingenuity, the creativity.

As I explained previously, the mathematical properties of the market are kryptonite for ML. Any genuinely honest exploration with proper validation, no-leakage, overfitting prevention methods, etc., will cause it to fail. The same for HMMs and GAs. To get these tools to work, if at all possible, requires a next level degree of ingenuity and out-of-the-box thinking.

The reflex to use ML is a reflex based on ignorance. People hope that their lack of understanding of finance can be supplemented by the God box that is ML. And so they neglect the theory, the fundamentals, everything, and deposit all trust into the God machine.
I could very easily build my GAs to have Sharpe >3.0. In fact, I even built one with Sharpe 3.7. But this collapses the moment it is applied live.

I've tried very very hard to get machine learning, genetic algorithms, and hidden Markov models to work. The results? Sharpe ratios identical to the SPY. More concretely: 0.6 - 0.8 over a 20 year history.
Likewise, ML is built for pattern recognition.
By design, market efficiency intends to destroy all patterns. As human beings, this is nigh-paradoxical, because our evolutionary mechanisms were built for pattern recognition.
As I learned about finance -- which is not my field -- I began to realize that the nonstationary regimes of finance were kryptonite to ML.

The trend strategy looked inferior for eight consecutive years. Then one crisis more than compensated for the entire period of lagging.

Consider this:

* SPY earns 12% annually for eight years, then loses 40%.
* A trend strategy earns only 10% annually for those eight years, then loses 10%.

After the eight good years and the crash:

* SPY turns $100 into about $149.
* The trend strategy turns $100 into about $193.
By avoiding the big crashes like 2000 and 2008, the overall total return outperforms the market because a -60% needs over 100% return to go back to where you were
But what it *does* do is reduce downside risk substantially
During bull runs, trend following can underperform the market, in fact a paper showed trend following underperforms the market 51% of the time
But this is not an absolute outperformance *at any time*
Yes, over the long run, moving average and trend following does return better than the market
